query: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exposed to the premelting and melting regime, the limited understanding of their thermal response prevents clear definition of their usable temperature range and behavior during high-temperature synthesis. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the onset and progression of their phase transition and why? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, relevant boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior nanoparticle studies, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The phase transition in FeNiCrCoCu HEA nanoparticles is initiated by a surface premelting mechanism: when heated near their depressed melting temperatures, the nanoparticle surfaces (with their high free energy and lower atomic coordination) locally melt to form a liquid-like shell that propagates inward, ultimately driving the entire particle into the molten state, facilitated by enhanced atomic diffusion resulting from multicomponent mixing.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid, crystalline FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles with homogeneous elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Expose the nanoparticles to controlled high-temperature treatment in an inert atmosphere with a careful temperature ramp through the premelting to melting regime.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under inert conditions (to prevent oxidation) and with controlled heating rates near the expected nanoparticle melting regime; a controlled comparison can be made with similarly sized bimetallic or lower-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
generation.structural_mediator: A liquid-like surface layer that forms on the nanoparticles as a result of reduced cohesive energy and melting point depression at the surface.
generation.mechanism: Due to their nanoscale dimensions and multicomponent nature, which introduces multicomponent mixing effects, the surface atoms of the FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles have lower coordination and altered bonding; this leads to a depressed local melting point so that, as the temperature increases, a thin liquid film (premelting) forms at the surface that facilitates enhanced atomic diffusion and further melting inward, thereby governing both the onset and progression of the complete phase transition.
generation.predicted_outcome: In situ high-resolution imaging and thermal analysis will reveal a distinct liquid-like layer on the surface of the nanoparticles at temperatures below the bulk melting point. As temperature increases, this liquid layer will thicken, eventually leading to complete melting. In comparison, lower-entropy or larger particles (with less pronounced melting point depression) will show either a delayed or less distinct surface premelting behavior.
generation.baseline: The intact, fully solid HEA nanoparticles characterized at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The nanoparticle system under inert atmosphere with controlled heating near the melting regime; results are restricted to nanoparticles of similar size (to minimize effects from size distribution) and under oxidation-free conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The exact onset temperature of surface melting and the kinetics of liquid layer propagation may depend on size variations, slight compositional inhomogeneities, and the precise heating rate. Quantitative details of the temperature window for premelting versus bulk melting remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Carry out in situ high-resolution TEM heating experiments on individual FeNiCrCoCu HEA nanoparticles while gradually increasing the temperature. Compare this with nanoparticles of similar size but lower elemental complexity. Use complementary techniques (e.g., electron energy loss spectroscopy) to monitor atomic diffusion and phase changes.
measurements: Direct visualization of a liquid-like surface layer forming prior to complete melting.
Measurement of the temperature at which this liquid shell appears versus the control sample.
Quantification of liquid layer thickness as a function of temperature.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no distinct surface liquid layer is observed before complete melting, or if the onset temperature and progression of melting in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are identical to those in lower-entropy or larger particles, then the hypothesis of surface premelting governing the phase transition is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This simple model of particle formation demonstrates that adding more elements innately promotes a more random nanoparticle, regardless of element interactions. Naturally, this model offers an idealized perspective and does not reflect all experimental details. In reality, there will be distinct mixing enthalpies between the elements. This will introduce a preference for certain structures which is opposed by the limited mobility of atoms. This explains how a rather mixed particle is obtained in the synthesis for a five-element mixture, which is restricted in the binary case, but also sees signs of local segregation in the NMF analysis. The model relates well to the single-source precursor synthesis, where a solid precursor is reduced at moderate temperatures, hence limiting the free mobility. Extending this approach to other syntheses with similar solid, mixed precursors can thus provide a viable way to design new low-temperature approaches for small high entropy alloy nanoparticles. It can further be argued that starting with a high number of different elements favors the exploration of high-entropy material spaces. As described above, during laser irradiation, the conversion of the HEA NPs from the mixed metal precursors adsorbed on LIG involves several processes, including thermal decomposition, metal ion reduction, metallic element melting, molten bead fusion, and fission, depending on the temperature experience. The laser synthesis in this work is based on solid-phase, which is different from liquid-phase synthesis. As the mixed metal precursor is adsorbed on the 3D porous LIG structure and dried before laser irradiation, the size of the nanoparticles can be well controlled by the laser fluence, and the concentration of the precursor due to the limited mobility of the reduced metal species and subsequently the nanoparticles.

Our work provides direct visualization of nanoparticles on amorphous carbon supports and elucidate the details of amorphous carbon graphitization during ultrafast exposure to extremely high temperatures under electrical Joule heating process. The in situ TEM studies of Joule heating on amorphous carbon fibers loaded with metal precursors show that during the Joule heating process, the CNFs undergo volumetric expansion due to amorphous to crystalline phase transition, which is also associated with formation and stabilization of metallic nanoparticles on the carbon supports. The crystallized CNFs are made of T-graphite with a high density of randomly dispersed edge planes. These edge planes are highly defective and act as preferred sites for the nucleation of metallic nanoparticles. In addition, metal atoms diffuse into layered structure strengthening the anchoring of the nanoparticles on the edge planes. This prevents the nanoparticles from further aggregation at extremely high temperatures as confirmed by MD simulation and in situ heating in TEM.
